Pregnancy

Ovarian cancer during pregnancy: making a coordinated care plan

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An ovarian mass found during pregnancy needs an explanation, but it is not automatically cancer. When cancer is suspected or confirmed, coordinated care can help you understand the next steps and the choices that affect both treatment and pregnancy.

An ovarian mass is not automatically cancer

Ovarian cancer is unusual during pregnancy, although it can be diagnosed at this time. Many ovarian masses found on a prenatal scan are benign. The fact that a scan describes a cyst, lump or mass does not by itself tell you whether it is cancer or what treatment it needs.

Ovarian cancer overall is more often diagnosed after menopause. In US statistics, about half of diagnoses occur at age 63 or older. Those population figures cannot calculate the chance that one pregnant person’s mass is malignant. A specialist considers the scan appearance, symptoms, changes over time and other findings together. Different ovarian tumor types also have different patterns and treatments.

Notice symptoms that persist or change

Early ovarian cancer may cause no obvious symptoms. When symptoms occur, they can overlap with pregnancy: persistent bloating, abdominal or pelvic pressure and pain, an upset stomach or heartburn, difficulty eating, or feeling full after a small amount of food. Needing to urinate more frequently or urgently, constipation, back discomfort and unusual fatigue may also be part of the picture.

These symptoms are much more often caused by something other than cancer. Nevertheless, tell your maternity clinician if they are new, persistent, worsening or different from your usual pregnancy symptoms. A normal-feeling abdomen does not rule out an ovarian mass. Equally, symptom severity alone cannot establish whether a mass is benign or malignant.

Seek urgent care for sudden severe abdominal pain, faintness or collapse, substantial bleeding or serious illness. A mass can occasionally cause urgent problems such as twisting, rupture or bleeding, even when it is not cancer. Do not wait for a routine oncology appointment if an acute problem develops.

Include your family history in the assessment

Mention ovarian, breast and other relevant cancers on both sides of your family, including the relative’s age at diagnosis and any known inherited gene result. Some ovarian cancers are associated with inherited changes such as BRCA1, BRCA2 or Lynch syndrome. Family history can influence genetic counselling and care, but its absence does not rule out cancer.

The NCI describes roughly one fifth of ovarian cancers overall as hereditary. Estimates depend on which tumors and populations are included; this is not a measure of your own risk during pregnancy. If cancer is confirmed, ask whether genetic testing is recommended for that tumor type and what the result could mean for treatment and relatives. A remembered family story is useful information, but it is not the same as a confirmed gene result.

Tests answer different questions

Assessment usually includes your history, an examination and ultrasound. A transvaginal scan may show an ovary in more detail, and an abdominal scan may also be useful. The clinician looks beyond size to the mass’s structure and other findings. Not every tumor can be felt during an examination, and one test may not provide the whole answer.

CA125 is a blood marker sometimes used in ovarian-cancer assessment. Pregnancy, inflammation and benign conditions can alter it, and some cancers do not produce a high result. A raised CA125 is therefore not a diagnosis, while a normal result is not an all-clear on its own. Ask how the result fits the imaging and whether repeating it would change management.

Non-contrast MRI can provide additional information when ultrasound leaves an important question unresolved. Necessary MRI is not automatically restricted to after the first trimester. Other imaging, including CT, may be appropriate when its clinical benefit warrants it. Your team should explain why the test is needed and how exposure is managed, rather than treating pregnancy as a reason to leave suspected cancer uninvestigated.

Confirmation usually requires a pathologist to examine tissue, often obtained at surgery. The safest method of obtaining it depends on the mass and the treatment plan. Do not assume that every suspicious ovary should have a needle biopsy. Ask what the pathology will establish, including the tumor type, and how the team will assess its extent.

Build one plan with the cancer and pregnancy teams

Care should bring together a gynecologic oncologist, your obstetric team and maternal-fetal medicine expertise, with other specialists such as an anesthetist and neonatal or pediatric team when needed. Ask which clinician coordinates the plan and whom to contact between appointments. A written summary can help when several services are involved.

Decisions depend on the cancer’s type and stage, how far the pregnancy has progressed, how urgently treatment is needed and your preferences about the pregnancy and future fertility. Treating your cancer effectively is central to care. The team also considers how to support the pregnancy and avoid preventable prematurity where possible.

Some situations permit treatment during pregnancy or a carefully justified delay; others require urgent treatment that changes the available pregnancy options. You should receive clear explanations of the expected benefit, the risks of delay and the uncertainties. There is no single choice that can be promised to be risk-free for every family.

Surgery and medicine have different timing considerations

Necessary cancer surgery should not be withheld or delayed solely because of pregnancy. A nonurgent procedure may be timed for a particular stage, but waiting until after birth is not the default for a confirmed cancer. Severe pain, bleeding, rupture or other complications may require an urgent operation. The extent of surgery depends on the tumor and what is needed for safe cancer care.

Some chemotherapy regimens can be used after the first trimester. SMFM generally recommends starting after 12 weeks when waiting until then will not meaningfully worsen the pregnant patient’s prognosis. This does not mean all drugs are suitable after that date. Exposure during early organ development raises particular concerns, and urgent treatment in early pregnancy requires a specialist discussion of the actual options.

Radiotherapy needs a separate assessment of the body area, dose and fetal exposure; pelvic treatment is especially problematic during an ongoing pregnancy. It is not a routine substitute for surgery or chemotherapy. Targeted and immune treatments also have their own restrictions and evidence gaps. Safety information about one medicine must not be applied to another.

Ask about support for nausea, pain, nutrition and prevention of blood clots, as well as the cancer treatment itself. Pregnancy and active cancer both affect care needs. Do not start, stop or substitute medicines or supplements without discussing them with the treating team.

Interpret child-outcome studies with care

A European study published in 2015 compared 129 children whose mothers had cancer during pregnancy with matched children whose mothers did not. Ninety-six in the exposed group had prenatal chemotherapy exposure, sometimes alongside other treatments. Early-childhood assessments did not find a significant overall cognitive difference between the groups. Premature birth was associated with poorer cognitive outcomes independently of treatment exposure.

That is reassuring evidence for carefully selected treatment, not a guarantee that every cancer medicine is harmless. The study involved several cancers and treatments, was not a randomized trial and did not establish lifelong outcomes for every exposed child. The specific regimen, pregnancy stage and reason for an early birth still matter.

A maternal cancer diagnosis does not mean the baby has cancer. However, it is too absolute to promise that cancer can never involve the placenta or fetus, or that the pregnancy cannot be affected. The team considers effects of illness, treatment and prematurity separately. Placental examination after birth is recommended in cancer pregnancies, and the baby’s clinician should know which treatments were given.

Coordinate monitoring and birth

Your team may arrange repeated ultrasound assessments of fetal growth and additional checks of wellbeing later in pregnancy. The timing depends on your cancer, treatment and obstetric findings. Ask how results will be shared and which symptoms, including a change in established fetal movements, require an immediate call.

Planned premature delivery is generally avoided unless there is a medical reason. Chemotherapy schedules usually allow a recovery interval before birth so that blood counts can recover; the interval depends on the drug. Cancer alone does not automatically require a cesarean. The obstetric situation and any planned cancer surgery should guide the delivery plan together.

The plan should also cover postpartum recovery, treatment resumption, practical help and emotional support. It can be difficult to manage a new baby and cancer appointments simultaneously. A support person, counselor or social worker may help you arrange transport, meals, childcare and time to rest.

Plan infant feeding around the actual medicines

The cancer diagnosis itself is different from medication exposure through breast milk. Breastfeeding is generally not recommended during cytotoxic chemotherapy because drugs can enter milk and harm the baby. Other cancer medicines and supportive treatments need their own review rather than being grouped together as simply strong or weak medicines.

If treatment has ended, the waiting time before breastfeeding depends on the drugs, their clearance and the clinical plan. There is no universal safe interval, and pumping does not make a medicine leave the body faster. Ask the oncology team and a feeding professional with medication expertise for written instructions. Formula or appropriately screened donor milk may be options while breast milk cannot be used; needing an alternative is not a failure.

Discuss future fertility before treatment when possible

The ovaries contain follicles and egg cells and produce hormones including estrogen and progesterone. Cancer can affect ovarian tissue, and treatment may require removal of one or both ovaries, sometimes with the uterus. Some chemotherapy and radiation treatments can damage remaining follicles or hormone function, causing temporary or permanent loss of fertility or early ovarian insufficiency.

Tell the team if future children are important to you before treatment begins, when possible. Selected tumors may allow fertility-preserving surgery, but this must not compromise cancer care. Egg, embryo or ovarian-tissue preservation is not automatically feasible during an existing pregnancy or in every ovarian cancer. Ask for a fertility specialist’s assessment of realistic choices rather than assuming a standard preservation procedure applies.

After treatment, advice about future pregnancy will depend on recovery, recurrence risk, the organs and ovarian function remaining, and any ongoing medicines. You can ask about these questions even when the immediate treatment decisions feel overwhelming. They belong in your care plan, alongside the pregnancy you are experiencing now.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Cancer and maternity specialists should plan investigations, treatment and delivery together.

Necessary treatment must be considered on its merits; reassuring studies do not establish safety for every medicine or every pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Keep your questions, medicine names and appointment plan together, and ask who coordinates decisions across the cancer and maternity teams.

When to seek help

Sudden severe abdominal pain, collapse, heavy bleeding or serious illness needs emergency assessment. During treatment, follow your oncology service’s urgent-contact instructions for fever or other new symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Most ovarian masses are not automatically malignant; specialist assessment determines the next step.
  • Symptoms can overlap with pregnancy, so persistent or worsening changes deserve attention.
  • CA125 and imaging inform assessment, while tissue establishes the diagnosis.
  • Treatment timing is individualized, and unnecessary prematurity is avoided where possible.
  • Feeding and future fertility need treatment-specific advice.

Frequently asked questions

Does an ovarian cyst during pregnancy mean cancer?

No. Many ovarian masses are benign. Ultrasound findings, symptoms and other information help specialists decide whether monitoring or further investigation is needed.

Can pregnancy symptoms hide ovarian cancer symptoms?

They can overlap. Persistent bloating, early fullness, pain or urinary and bowel changes should be discussed rather than automatically attributed to pregnancy.

Can CA125 confirm or rule out ovarian cancer?

No. Pregnancy and benign conditions can raise it, and some cancers do not. It must be interpreted alongside imaging and the clinical assessment.

Must MRI wait until after the first trimester?

Not automatically. Non-contrast MRI can be used when clinically indicated. The team chooses the investigation that answers the important question with appropriate precautions.

Should cancer surgery always wait until after birth?

No. Necessary surgery should not be delayed solely because of pregnancy. Timing and the operation itself depend on the tumor, urgency and pregnancy circumstances.

Is all chemotherapy safe after 12 weeks?

No. Some regimens may be appropriate after the first trimester, but each drug and situation needs specialist assessment. A gestational date alone does not establish safety.

Do reassuring child studies guarantee no later effects?

No. They support careful treatment choices but have limits in the cancers, drugs and ages studied. Your team should explain the evidence for your actual regimen.

Will I automatically need an early cesarean?

No. Birth timing and mode depend on obstetric and cancer-related needs. Avoiding unnecessary prematurity is an important part of planning.

Can I breastfeed during chemotherapy?

Breastfeeding is generally not recommended during cytotoxic chemotherapy. Ask about your exact medicines and the waiting interval before milk can safely be used.

Can treatment affect future pregnancies?

Yes. Surgery and some medicines or radiation can affect eggs, hormones or the ability to carry a pregnancy. Discuss fertility goals before treatment when possible.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
